title: The seer of the Gayatri
hookLine: a king loses to a sage's staff, becomes a seer himself, and the verse prayed at dawn and dusk is credited to him
carry: sandhya: prayer at the joints of the day
tomorrow: what mantra does every breath already say?

lines: A KING WANTS THE SAGE'S COW.
EVERY WEAPON SWALLOWED BY A STAFF.
A SAGE'S STRENGTH IS REAL STRENGTH.
cards: A king named Vishvamitra rides with his army into a forest hermitage and sees the sage Vasishtha's wonderful cow, the one who can give anything. He wants her. He offers thousands of cows, elephants, gold.
Vasishtha won't part with her. The king tries to take her by force, and she brings forth armies that rout his.
He goes off and wins divine weapons by austerity, comes back, and turns them on the sage himself, and every one is swallowed by a single thing: Vasishtha's wooden staff.
The king looks at his empty hands and says: shame on a warrior's strength; a sage's strength is the real strength.

teach.b: That's the Ramayana, in its first book.

The king sets down his crown and begins tapas, a long austerity that runs, in the telling, thousands of years, through failures, temper and temptation, until Vasishtha himself calls him a brahmarshi, a sage of the highest rank.
And to this seer the tradition credits one of the most loved verses in Hinduism.
It's in the third book of the Rig Veda, the book of Vishvamitra's family, and it's called the Gayatri, or the Savitri, after Savitr, the divine sun who stirs the world awake.

teach.h: THE GAYATRI: MAY IT STIR OUR MINDS.
teach.b: Its prayer, in paraphrase: we meditate on the bright glory of the divine sun; may it stir our minds. Not a prayer for a win, or a crop, or a kingdom. For understanding.
A king who learned his weapons were nothing next to a sage's insight gives the world a prayer for light in the mind. Here's the practice built around it.

teach.h: STAND AT DAWN, SIT AT DUSK.
teach.b: The Manusmriti, one of the old books of dharma, says: at dawn, stand repeating the Savitri until the sun is seen; at dusk, sit repeating it until the stars appear.

teach.h: SANDHYA: THE JOINTS OF THE DAY.
teach.b: The joints of the day are called sandhya, a joining, and the rite kept at them is called sandhya too. In many families it's tied to the sacred-thread initiation, and the verse is learned from a teacher.
But anyone can see what the timing teaches: prayer belongs at the hinges, where night turns to day and day to night. The light itself keeps the time.

how: Many Hindu families keep sandhya, a rite at dawn and dusk built around the Gayatri, credited to the seer Vishvamitra; some who keep a mantra sadhana tie their own japa to those same hinges of the day.

o: a mantra said on the hour, every hour, by the clock
a prayer for victory, said before a battle
prayer kept at the joints of the day, dawn and dusk

games.q: the king, the verse and the light — tap the pairs.
p: the king who became a seer
may the divine light stir our minds

s: the Gayatri is a prayer for wealth and victory
in paraphrase it asks the divine sun to stir our minds: a prayer for understanding.
sandhya names both the joints of the day and the rite kept at them
the word means a joining, and the dawn and dusk rite carries the same name.
in the Manusmriti, the morning recitation is done sitting
it says to stand at dawn until the sun is seen, and to sit at dusk.

games.q: your roommate sees you at the window at sunrise, murmuring a mantra, and asks why that exact minute and not after breakfast. what fits today's teaching?
o: it's a hinge of the day, a sandhya, where Hindus have long kept the Gayatri at dawn and dusk.
no reason, it's just when the alarm went off.
the mantra only works while the sun is low.
games.why: the Manusmriti sets the Savitri, the Gayatri, at the sandhya: stand at dawn until the sun shows, sit at dusk until the stars appear. the joints of the day are for prayer.

practice: Notice the light where you are right now, morning, afternoon or evening, then begin your own mantra, silently or in a whisper, and let it run.
As it runs, choose your hinge, the first light or the last, where the mantra will start tomorrow: when the light changes, not when a free moment turns up.

wordCard.voice: Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, its when: the sandhya, the joints of the day, where Vishvamitra's verse is kept at dawn and dusk.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sandhya, a joining; the twilights of the day and the rite kept at them.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: sandhya, prayer at the joints of the day. A king put down his weapons and gave the world a prayer for light. See you tomorrow.
